segments.title: Why Germany kept building torpedo boats
segments.body: Germany's attachment to torpedo boats developed through coastal, divisional, and larger fleet craft, with several reasons for retaining the concept. Gröner's two-volume reference supplies the broad account of German ship designs used here. Alex Clarke recommends it while disagreeing with some interpretations: historians can accept the same facts and weigh their significance differently. His approach gives particular weight to engineering choices and actual expenditure, which record what a navy committed resources to building. Official explanations can contain part of the truth while leaving other motives unstated.

evidence.note: The coastal-to-large-boat sequence and the multiple reasons for retaining the torpedo-boat concept.
Gröner's broad coverage of German naval designs and its use as a reference.
Clarke's explanation of differing historical interpretations and his preference for funded engineering choices when testing official justifications.

segments.summary: Germany's coastal, divisional, and ocean-going boats reveal how operational needs and funding politics kept the torpedo-boat concept alive.

segments.title: British-built boats helped Germany test the concept
segments.body: Germany bought early torpedo boats from experienced British builders while developing its own designs. The 1884 examples include Thornycroft, Yarrow, and J. S. White alongside Weser, Vulcan, and Schichau. These purchases tested the torpedo-boat concept during the transition away from spar torpedoes. Studying British boats let German yards and crews adapt ideas from a navy with longer experience of building and operating the type. Purchases of British-built vessels continued because that comparison remained useful.

evidence.note: British and German builders supplied early concept-test boats as Germany moved beyond spar torpedoes and studied more experienced builders.
German examination of useful British design features and weaknesses, and continued purchases of British-built boats.

segments.summary: Early German orders from Thornycroft, Yarrow, and White supplied proven ideas while domestic yards learned what a useful torpedo boat should be.

segments.title: Why navies copied Royal Navy port-visit procedures
segments.body: Navies copied established operating procedures as well as hardware. Royal Navy port visits offered examples of diplomatic rules, the order of proceedings, and the practical handling of an overseas visit. Reusing those arrangements saved officers from negotiating every detail from scratch. A navy visiting somewhere for the first time could still adapt an established method to the new setting. German study of British torpedo boats followed the same logic of learning from earlier experience and mistakes.

evidence.note: Copying tested procedures and avoiding earlier mistakes, illustrated by Royal Navy port visits and then applied to German torpedo-boat technology.

segments.summary: Port-visit protocols illustrate why a navy could borrow British practice for practical reasons while adapting it to its own needs.

segments.title: Why German torpedo boats carried numbers, not names
segments.body: T16, S42, and S82 illustrate Germany's use of letter-and-number designations for torpedo boats. These craft were treated as boats and received numbers rather than individual ship names. S42 is identified as an S7-class boat and S82 as an S66-class boat. The naming system prioritized efficient identification, while the early class groupings were less tidy than later readers might expect.

evidence.note: T16, S42 of the S7 class, and S82 of the S66 class illustrate numbered boats and the treatment of class labels.

segments.summary: Designations such as T16, S42, and S82 reflect a service that treated these craft as numbered boats and did not always impose tidy class groupings.

segments.title: Coastal boats freed larger ships for other duties
segments.body: The Franco-Prussian War left Germany with a recognized need for a navy, while the navy's precise tasks remained open to debate. Cheap torpedo boats could protect ports and coasts, freeing larger warships to operate elsewhere. Many early boats survived into World War I as minesweepers, school boats, and tenders. Their torpedoes still complicated an enemy's Baltic plans, since even obsolete craft took time to suppress and could add to the volume of an attack. Age and limited speed reduced their value, so continued service did not make them suitable front-line fleet units.

evidence.note: Port defence released larger assets for other duties, and early boats later served as minesweepers, school boats, and tenders.
Old boats still carried torpedoes that complicated Baltic operations, despite limited speed and ageing expansion engines.

segments.summary: Small German torpedo boats began as inexpensive coastal and port defenders that could release larger warships for operations elsewhere.

segments.title: The coastal boats built from 1914 remained small defenders
segments.body: The coastal boats built from 1914 continued the small, inexpensive defensive concept. At roughly 100-110 tons, they used coal-fired expansion machinery for about 20 knots and a maximum range of 900 nautical miles at 12.5 knots. Fewer than 30 crew operated a single light deck gun, two 450 mm torpedoes, and some mines. Their deck-gun calibre is given as 50 or 52 mm depending on the weapon fitted. The totals cited are 92 completed from 113 planned and 30 lost, mostly during World War I. Survivors served in the Polish, Belgian, Estonian, and Soviet navies, some until 1950. These useful coastal craft reinforced the political expectation that torpedo boats would remain cheap.

evidence.note: The separate 1914-onward coastal type, disputed destroyer label, machinery, performance, weapons, construction totals, and later foreign service.
Cheap torpedo boats established a lasting expectation among politicians.

segments.summary: Small hulls, short range, and light armament explain the coastal role of boats whose survivors served several navies after World War I.

segments.title: Fleet service forced torpedo boats to grow
segments.body: The divisional torpedo boats launched between 1886 and 1898 tested ideas that led to larger German torpedo craft. Their development overlapped with Britain's early Daring, Havoc, and Ferret destroyers. Fleet commanders began to want torpedo boats alongside their larger ships, which placed new demands on endurance and seakeeping. A boat defending a port could wait for an attacker, while a vessel accompanying the fleet had to reach the area where enemy torpedo craft operated. Fleet service therefore pushed hull size beyond what local defence alone required.

evidence.note: Divisional boats developed between 1886 and 1898 alongside early British destroyers and served as proving grounds for larger German craft.
Operating divisional boats with the fleet exposed the need to travel and remain at sea, driving size growth.

segments.summary: Divisional boats exposed a basic design pressure: craft expected to accompany a fleet needed enough size, endurance, and seaworthiness to stay with it.

segments.title: D10 combined a British hull with German weapons
segments.body: D10 came from Thornycroft's British 30-knotter design but carried a German armament. Its battery comprised three 50 mm guns and three 450 mm torpedo tubes. Each tube had one torpedo, with no reloads carried. A crew of 47-52 served a boat of about 370 tons fully loaded, with a quoted top speed of 27.2 knots. That made D10 a capable vessel for its time, while leaving little room for the demands of prolonged fleet service.

evidence.note: D10's Thornycroft origin, German battery, absence of reloads, crew range, quoted speed, and full-load displacement. The gun's L/40 designation is recalled tentatively.

segments.summary: D10's three torpedoes without reloads, modest hull, and quoted 27.2-knot speed show the limits of an early fleet torpedo boat.

segments.title: Small carried boats faced seakeeping and maintenance limits
segments.body: Germany experimented with small torpedo boats carried aboard larger warships and launched when needed. The idea proved less attractive in practice than on paper, encouraging boats that could keep themselves at sea. The comparison raises an open question about small uncrewed surface vessels: exercises may reveal similar launch, recovery, and endurance problems. Without a crew aboard, maintenance is harder to perform at sea. Adding enough redundant systems to survive failures also increases the vessel's size. Fleet boats needed to stay with the force without being lost in rough seas or towed home.

evidence.note: Carried torpedo boats and the speculative comparison with uncrewed craft, including recovery, maintenance, and the size cost of redundancy.
Fleet boats had to remain at sea without requiring a tow or being lost in waves.

segments.summary: The failed appeal of carried torpedo boats prompts a cautious comparison with modern uncrewed craft and their maintenance requirements.

segments.title: Low prestige gave torpedo-boat designers room to diverge
segments.body: One criticism of Tirpitz's naval policy is that it encouraged a miniature Royal Navy, with Germany acquiring ship categories because Britain had them. Torpedo boats sat lower in the prestige hierarchy, so senior personalities paid less attention to their exact design choices. That neglect gave designers room to tailor light craft to German operational needs. Support for building torpedo boats did not require copying British destroyers feature for feature.

evidence.note: The interpretation that low-status torpedo boats escaped some of the pressure to copy Royal Navy force structure.

segments.summary: Because torpedo boats were not prestige assets, their designers had more freedom to suit German needs instead of copying the Royal Navy feature for feature.

segments.title: Army budgets kept the cheap-boat idea alive
segments.body: Competition with the Army constrained the Kaiserliche Marine's light forces as well as its capital ships. Naval spending competed for money that could fund Army equipment and research, and the Army remained Germany's primary force. The cheap torpedo boat offered a politically attractive counter to larger British destroyers. Yet the size comparison concealed different missions: British boats were built for worldwide service, while German designs concentrated on the North Sea. In this interpretation, budget allocation also restricted the industrial capacity Germany could have developed, so the constraint went beyond existing yard capacity.

evidence.note: Army-Navy budget competition, the scope for funded industrial expansion, the cheap-boat argument, and differing British and German operating requirements.

segments.summary: Domestic competition with the German Army made torpedo boats attractive as supposedly cheap counters to larger, globally deployable British destroyers.

segments.title: Army budget pressure closed Germany's naval spending contest
segments.body: Rising battleship costs intensified the conflict between German naval ambitions and Army funding. Pressure had grown from about 1905 and reached a limit around 1913, when the Army insisted that naval increases could no longer come at its expense. Germany's land borders made the Army's claim difficult to displace. This reading treats domestic budget politics as the point at which Germany lost the naval spending race. The V25 belongs to the ensuing search for ways to operate against the Royal Navy after further escalation had become politically untenable.

evidence.note: Rising battleship costs, Army resistance from about 1905, the 1913 funding limit, and pressure to rethink the risk-fleet approach.

segments.summary: The rising cost of competing with Britain forced German naval planners to confront the Army's priority in domestic funding.

segments.title: The S90 made the torpedo boat an offensive fleet arm
segments.body: The S90s were large beside contemporary British destroyers, but they were slower and initially less heavily gunned. A crew of 69 operated three 450 mm torpedo tubes and an early battery of three 50 mm guns. Forty-eight boats were built, and some remained in service with Germany or other operators in 1921. The design concentrated on delivering torpedoes from a stable platform, making these boats an offensive skirmishing arm. An analogy with light cavalry explains their intended role: influencing the information picture and the shape of a battle while avoiding direct combat with the enemy's strongest units.

evidence.note: S90 displacement, speed, crew and armament compared with British destroyers, followed by the construction total and long service.
Stable offensive torpedo platforms and the light-cavalry analogy for shaping information and the battlefield.

segments.summary: The 544-ton S90 class traded British-style gun weight and extreme speed for a stable torpedo platform intended to shape a fleet engagement.

segments.title: How did the S90 compare with British turbine destroyers?
segments.body: Contemporary British destroyers were smaller than the S90s and placed much greater emphasis on speed. The Viper comparison combines Parsons turbines with a displacement of about 350 tons, rising to about 400 tons fully loaded. Its battery comprised one 12-pounder, five 6-pounders, and two torpedo tubes. The S90s made 28 knots and carried 69 crew, almost the same complement as the 68 men crowded into the smaller British boat.

evidence.note: S90 and Viper displacement, speed priorities, armament, and nearly equal crews. Viper's exact speed is unclear in the captions.

segments.summary: The S90 was a larger torpedo platform, while Viper emphasized turbine speed and gun armament in a smaller hull.
segments.question: How did the S90 compare with contemporary Royal Navy destroyers?
segments.answerShort: The S90 was larger and slower, while the smaller British turbine boats carried stronger gun batteries and nearly the same number of crew.

segments.title: G132 and G135 explored different gun batteries
segments.body: The G132 and G135 groups sit between the main S90 run and the S138 evolution. Their different gun arrangements suggest trials for the later S138 design, although that connection is an interpretation. One group carried four 52 mm guns, while the other combined an 88 mm gun with lighter pieces. Both retained three 450 mm torpedo tubes, so the changes explored greater gun power within a design still centered on torpedo attack.

evidence.note: Different G132 and G135 gun arrangements with three 450 mm torpedo tubes, with their possible role as S138 trials presented as an interpretation.

segments.summary: The G132 and G135 groups retained three 450 mm torpedo tubes while trying different gun batteries, suggesting a bridge between the S90 and S138 designs.

segments.title: The S138 label concealed a design revolution
segments.body: The S138 series began near 684 tons fully loaded and eventually reached roughly 824 tons. Its first boats were already 140 tons heavier than the 544-ton S90. Batches built between 1906 and 1911 changed machinery and armament during a period of rapid naval development. Later boats carried four 500 mm torpedo tubes in place of the early three 450 mm tubes. One class name therefore covered boats with different performance and fighting capability.

evidence.note: S138 full-load displacement grew from 684 to 824 tons after the 544-ton S90.
Changing boilers, propulsion, sustained speed, crews, and weapons across S138 batches built during 1906-1911.

segments.summary: Successive S138 batches grew, adopted turbines and oil firing, and changed armament so extensively that one class name obscured several distinct designs.

segments.title: Why Royal Navy destroyers grew beyond the S138s
segments.body: As the S138 batches grew, Royal Navy destroyers first caught and then surpassed them in displacement. River-class boats were already roughly 640 tons, while the contemporary Tribals reached about 982 tons deep load. British requirements combined global deployment with the need to destroy larger, better-subdivided German craft. German planners optimized for North Sea operations and preserved the political image of the cheap torpedo boat, with Jeune Ecole ideas still in the background. Displacement reflected operational requirements and the political limits on German naval expenditure.

evidence.note: S138 growth compared with River- and Tribal-class destroyers, including the need for British guns to defeat larger German boats.
British global requirements, Germany's North Sea focus, and the political appeal of supposedly cheap torpedo boats.

segments.summary: British destroyer growth reflected global operations and the need to defeat larger German boats, while German cheap-boat politics restrained displacement.

segments.title: Cruiser cuts weakened German torpedo-boat support at Jutland
segments.body: Keeping torpedo boats cheap did not solve the wider fleet-balance problem. German cruiser construction was cut, so at Jutland its light forces faced more British destroyers and a much larger supporting cruiser force. Those cruisers stiffened and supported Royal Navy flotillas, worsening an already unfavorable numbers problem. Comparing destroyer and torpedo-boat totals alone therefore understates the German disadvantage.

evidence.note: Curtailed German cruiser construction and British superiority in destroyers and supporting cruisers at Jutland.

segments.summary: German torpedo boats faced more British destroyers at Jutland and a much larger cruiser force supporting them.

segments.title: Different S138 machinery complicated flotilla maneuvers
segments.body: Successive S138 batches changed from four coal-fired boilers to three coal-fired boilers and one oil-fired boiler. Propulsion also shifted from two-shaft triple-expansion machinery to turbines on two and then three shafts. Nominal top speeds of roughly 30-32 knots concealed differences in how well the boats maintained speed on trials. Turbine boats performed better in this respect than some of the reciprocating-engine boats. Those differences raised doubts about maneuvering the earliest and latest batches together, even though they shared a class designation.

evidence.note: Changing S138 boilers and propulsion, nominal versus sustained trial speed, and doubts about maneuvering early and late batches together.

segments.summary: Early and late S138 batches differed in machinery and sustained speed, complicating their use together in formation.

segments.title: Why were the S138 batches called one class?
segments.body: Later S138 batches had different hull arrangements, machinery, weapons, and even an additional funnel. S182 makes the difference visible through its second funnel, rearranged masts, and altered hull. The funding argument is that retaining a familiar designation made repeat orders easier to present without inviting close scrutiny of the changes. Parts of the navy treated the batches as different classes, while historians continued the grouping found in the documents. In this reading, the shared label reflects administrative and political convenience despite substantial technical differences.

evidence.note: The explicit question of why the differing batches were all grouped as S138s.
S182's altered funnels, masts, and hull support the argument that funding and documentary continuity sustained the shared class label.

segments.summary: The argument for retaining the S138 label centers on easier funding and documentary continuity despite substantial changes between batches.
segments.question: Why did the Kaiserliche Marine group the very different S138 batches as one class?
segments.answerShort: Keeping one designation made repeat funding easier, and historians continued the documentary grouping even though the boats differed substantially.

segments.title: Arleigh Burke upgrades within an inherited design
segments.body: Arleigh Burke Flights I and III illustrate major technological changes within one named class. The criticism is that their equipment developed much further than the underlying design and architecture. Successive upgrades required later systems to work within arrangements not originally designed to support them. The case for a replacement rests on providing a hull whose design supports the infrastructure required by newer systems more efficiently.

evidence.note: The argument that successive Arleigh Burke upgrades leave newer systems constrained by inherited architecture and justify a replacement.

segments.summary: The Arleigh Burke comparison explains the argument for a replacement hull architecture to support newer systems more efficiently.

segments.title: S138 torpedo growth followed larger targets
segments.body: Successive S138 batches moved from three 450 mm torpedo tubes to four 500 mm tubes. The progression included a brief 460 mm stage. Both calibre and tube count increased, producing a substantial rise in striking power. That growth reflected the increasing size of the ships the torpedo boats were expected to stop.

evidence.note: S138 torpedo growth from three 450 mm tubes through a brief 460 mm stage to four 500 mm tubes, related to larger targets.

segments.summary: The S138 evolution increased torpedo calibre and tube count as the intended targets grew larger.

segments.title: The V1 class sacrificed capability for cheap mass
segments.body: After the steady growth of the S138 batches, the V1 class reversed course to a 570-ton hull carrying four 500 mm torpedo tubes and two 88 mm guns. Wilhelm von Lans pushed the design through because he believed small, inexpensive boats could supply numerical strength. Contemporary British destroyers carried heavier gun batteries, while the experimental HMS Swift showed how much larger a destroyer could become. The V1s proved poor sea boats and unstable platforms for their torpedoes as well as their guns. Two were sold to Greece as counters to larger S138-derived boats sold to the Ottoman Empire. Despite the V1s' newer design, the preference expressed here is for the larger Ottoman boats.

evidence.note: The 570-ton V1 design, Lans's cheap-mass argument, its weapons, British comparisons, and poor seakeeping and stability.
The sale of two V1s to Greece, preference for the larger Ottoman S138-derived boats, and the judgment that V1 represented a regression.

segments.summary: Vice Admiral Wilhelm von Lans forced the 570-ton V1 design toward cheap numerical strength, producing boats with weak seakeeping and gun power.

segments.title: V1 economy retained large crews and weak guns
segments.body: The appeal of the V1 lay in cheap torpedo craft that could offset an enemy's numerical advantage and be risked in close action. Small crews were part of that argument, although losing a boat was still undesirable. A V1 actually carried 74 people, close to the complement of much larger late S138 variants. The gun choice was also weak: the class received the 88 mm L/30, designed in 1892, when better 88 mm weapons existed. The criticism is that commitment to the small torpedo-boat concept outweighed an assessment of what the vessels needed to fight effectively.

evidence.note: Cheap, expendable torpedo craft contrasted with the V1 complement of 74, close to that of much larger late S138 variants.
The older 88 mm L/30 design and criticism of an admiral's commitment to the small torpedo-boat concept.

segments.summary: The supposedly expendable V1s still needed 74 crew and carried an 88 mm L/30 gun designed in 1892.

segments.title: Construction and survivability separate destroyers from torpedo boats
segments.body: In this interpretation, large German torpedo boats were not interchangeable with destroyers. A torpedo boat concentrated on high speed and torpedo attack, while a destroyer was built to fight another small combatant. Different internal subdivision reflected that distinction in purpose. Both could carry powerful weapons without being able to withstand equivalent damage, but the destroyer was expected to survive a glancing hit and continue fighting. Technological change complicates comparisons: a torpedo boat from 1906 or 1907 could outclass a destroyer from the 1890s without sharing its original design priorities.

evidence.note: Different construction, internal subdivision, and fighting purposes, illustrated through the ability to survive glancing hits.
A newer torpedo boat can outclass an older destroyer because light-warship technology changed rapidly.

segments.summary: Destroyers and torpedo boats differed in construction and fighting purpose, while rapid technological change could let a newer torpedo boat outclass an older destroyer.

segments.title: Wegener challenged the High Seas Fleet's North Sea focus
segments.body: Wolfgang Wegener, senior staff officer to Wilhelm von Lans while Lans commanded the High Seas Fleet's First Squadron, criticized Germany's prewar naval armament and strategy. His paper argued that the Baltic should receive priority because it carried the Swedish iron ore supply route. Lans left his post in 1915 and went onto the reserve list. His influence as inspector of torpedoes from 1909 to 1912 had already affected the boats Germany bought. The criticism of his command style is that fleet leadership required strategic and political flexibility that his commitment to his own ideas did not provide.

evidence.note: Wegener's Baltic argument, Lans's removal in 1915, criticism of his strategic rigidity, and his influence as inspector of torpedoes in 1909-12. No direct causal link between the paper and removal is established.
Wolfgang Wegener's name is recalled tentatively and then checked and confirmed.

segments.summary: Wolfgang Wegener's paper argued that Germany undervalued the Baltic and its Swedish iron-ore route by treating the North Sea as the primary theater.

segments.title: Foreign orders enabled Germany's largest torpedo boats
segments.body: The move toward truly large German torpedo boats drew on assets intended for other navies. The G101s originated with Argentine orders and approached 1,850 tons fully loaded. The B97s approached 1,750 tons and used machinery ordered for the Imperial Russian Navy's next generation of destroyers. War prevented delivery to Russia, leaving German yards able to offer that machinery to the Kaiserliche Marine. These foreign orders helped supply the larger boats needed after the disappointing V1 experiment.

evidence.note: The G101s' Argentine origin and near-1,850-ton displacement, and the B97s' near-1,750-ton displacement and Russian-ordered machinery retained after war began.

segments.summary: Argentine orders supplied the G101 type, while machinery ordered for Russia enabled the B97s and helped Germany obtain larger boats.

segments.title: Torpedoes were meant to finish Germany's fleet ambush
segments.body: The High Seas Fleet was supposed to isolate part of the Grand Fleet and destroy it before British reinforcements arrived. Torpedo boats would deliver the rapid killing attack because a prolonged battleship duel could cost German capital ships and give the rest of the British fleet time to intervene. The smaller craft were considered more expendable and, at least theoretically, quicker to replace. Japan's later World War II attrition plan similarly aimed to reduce an approaching enemy fleet to parity or inferiority before winning a decisive battle and dictating peace. Germany could use its own improvement in the balance of forces either to negotiate from strength or to seek another victorious battle. The vulnerable assumption was that Britain would allow a detached force to be isolated and destroyed.

evidence.note: Torpedo boats as theoretically replaceable killing forces in an ambush that must end before British reinforcements arrive.
Japanese attrition comparison, Germany's alternatives of peace negotiation or further battle, and criticism of relying on British fleet separation.

segments.summary: German plans expected torpedo boats to deliver rapid killing blows after an isolated portion of the Grand Fleet had been trapped.

segments.title: Why torpedoes promised a rapid fleet decision
segments.body: Torpedoes promised to make a ship sink quickly by opening it below the waterline. The simplified damage distinction is between fire the crew cannot extinguish and flooding through a hole the crew cannot close. Letting air into a ship does not produce the same result. A torpedo's ability to create uncontrollable flooding therefore suited the demand for a rapid killing blow.

evidence.note: Uncontrollable fire and flooding as ship-loss mechanisms, with torpedoes offering a rapid way to create fatal underwater damage.

segments.summary: A torpedo could produce a rapid decision by causing flooding that the target's crew could not contain.

segments.title: What if the German fleet ambush became a brawl?
segments.body: A battle that became a brawl would force German torpedo boats to fight off British destroyers. Those destroyers could also draw on extensive light-cruiser support. Germany's limited cruiser construction left it short of comparable assistance for its own boats. That prospect demanded changes in the light forces Germany built, since a quick torpedo strike alone would not answer the threat.

evidence.note: The explicit question about a brawling battle and the need to fight British destroyers supported by numerous light cruisers.

segments.summary: A prolonged melee would force German torpedo boats to fight British destroyers backed by light cruisers, exposing Germany's weak cruiser support.
segments.question: How could German torpedo boats cope if the planned fleet ambush became a prolonged brawl?
segments.answerShort: They would need to fight through British destroyers and their strong light-cruiser support, a task for which Germany lacked enough comparable screening ships.

segments.title: The V25 correction came after the naval race ended
segments.body: The V1 experience clarified that Germany needed larger, more capable boats, and the V25 class provided that answer. Yet the realization arrived in 1912-13, just as Army pressure closed the financial contest with Britain. Of the eventual 71 boats, 57 were built during World War I and 62 were lost during the conflict. Only 32 were in service by Jutland, so limited availability prevented the class from replacing the older flotillas at once.

evidence.note: The V1 experience exposed the failure of the small-boat policy, but the realization came as Army pressure closed the naval spending race.
The V25 figures given are 71 built, 57 during World War I, 62 lost during the war, and 32 in service by Jutland.

segments.summary: The capable V25 class corrected the V1 experiment, but most boats arrived during World War I and could not repair the prewar force structure in time.

segments.title: Which torpedo boats could Germany take to Jutland?
segments.body: Germany took 61 torpedo boats to Jutland, so choosing the newest boats did not mean choosing only the most capable designs: the recent V1s were among them. The wider comparison lists 155 large torpedo boats, of which Germany retained 149 after selling two to Greece and four to the Ottomans; 92 were turbine powered. Eighteen additional V25s entered service between 1914 and Jutland in time to work up. A couple more commissioned in May 1916 raise a separate question about readiness. Maintenance and servicing could keep a commissioned boat out of an operation, so Germany could not assume that every V25 would sail. The V1s provided available numbers despite poor seakeeping and limited capability. The battlecruiser scouting force also included V25s and the Argentine-derived G101s.

evidence.note: The fleet-selection question includes the newer but poorly regarded V1s.
Fleet totals, 18 additional V25s worked up before Jutland, May 1916 commissioning doubts, and limits on operational availability.
V25 flotillas and V25/G101 boats accompanying the battlecruiser scouting force.

segments.summary: Germany's 61 torpedo boats at Jutland included V25s, Argentine-derived G101s, and weaker V1s, with selection constrained by operational availability.
segments.question: Which torpedo boats could Germany actually take to the Battle of Jutland?
segments.answerShort: A mixed force of V25s, G101s, and V1s, constrained by work-up, maintenance, and service requirements.

segments.title: Why the V1s accompanied the High Seas Fleet
segments.body: The V1s accompanied the High Seas Fleet even though their design attracts sustained criticism. One interpretation is that they were the boats Germany could most readily sacrifice if a torpedo attack was needed to let the main fleet escape. Earlier S138 boats remained on other duties. Those included Baltic operations and North Sea work against the Harwich Force and Channel Barrage.

evidence.note: Proposed V1 sacrifice to cover a withdrawal, with earlier boats assigned to Baltic and other North Sea duties.
V1 expendability is presented as an interpretation reached after examining the plans.

segments.summary: One explanation for taking the V1s to Jutland is that Germany could risk losing them to cover a withdrawal, while older boats served elsewhere.

segments.title: Were Germany's large torpedo boats really destroyers?
segments.body: The proposed distinction between a large torpedo boat and a destroyer is the emphasis placed on gun armament. A torpedo boat is built around torpedoes as its dominant weapon. A period destroyer gives guns and torpedoes a more balanced relationship, with torpedoes first among equals. On that definition, increasing a torpedo boat's size does not automatically make it a destroyer.

evidence.note: Destroyers distinguished from torpedo boats by the design's emphasis on guns relative to torpedoes.

segments.summary: Gun armament supplies the proposed dividing line: torpedoes dominate a torpedo boat's design, while destroyers give their guns a greater role.
segments.question: Were Germany's large torpedo boats really destroyers, and did the distinction matter?
segments.answerShort: On the distinction proposed here, they remained torpedo boats when torpedoes dominated the design; destroyers gave guns a greater role alongside them.
